Drummer Jake Hanna has been the spark plug behind some of this country’s hottest jazz ensembles. A native of Boston, he was born on April 4, 1931 and received his first drum lessons from Stanley Spector. In the mid 50s, Jake played with a succession of jazz stars including Woody Herman, Marian McPartland and Maynard Ferguson. He has had a steady career on both coasts, moving to Los Angeles in 1970 with the Merv Griffin Show. His lengthy list of recordings include work with SuperSax, Oscar Peterson, Herb Ellis and Carl Fontana.
Jake is the subject of a chapter in Marian McPartland’s book All in Good Time. He continues to lead a busy schedule of recording and appearances at jazz clubs and festivals.
Jake was interviewed at the Jerome Jazz Party in Aspen, Colorado on October 11, 1997, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

We are in Aspen, Colorado, filming for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive. And I’ve been waiting for this for quite a while now. We’re filming with Jake Hanna, one of the great jazz drummers and conversationalists.

Conversationalist, yes. I love your name, Monk. I’m going to start using that name, Monk Rowe. I’ve been using Sneed Hern for years. But Monk Rowe, that’s a hell of a name. I never heard a name like that either. Thelonious Monk was far out, but Monk Rowe.
I’ll be expecting some checks in the mail though if you start to do that I think.
Oh, yeah, yeah, good. I’ll send you back yours if it bounces to me it’ll bounce back to you. Sounds like basketball.
Oh, my. I’m going to read something here—
Okay? That you told to a very famous lady. You had three childhood heroes: Brace Beemer—
Brace Beemer, The Lone Ranger. Ross Tompkins knows him.
